title: Returning to the source
hook: renewers kept returning to the Qur'an and sunnah

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer never stopped: fixed hours tied to the sun, outlasting the courts. Your line was the prayer went on. Did you keep the moment you chose? Day one thousand fifty-six.

A river runs through a town. By the time it reaches the market it has picked up a lot along the way: soil from the fields, leaves, whatever the streets wash into it. Someone wants to know what the water was like at the start, and there are two ways to find out. Study it where it runs past you. Or walk upstream, past the town, past the fields, up into the hills, until you reach the spring where it comes out of the rock. The water there hasn't passed through anybody yet. This path has met a lot of reformers this year, in very different places and times. Look closely at what they did, and they keep walking upstream. Today: returning to the source.
screen: `A MUDDY RIVER THROUGH A TOWN.` → `FILTER IT, OR WALK UPSTREAM?` → `THE SPRING IN THE ROCK.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction is in the Qur'an itself. When believers disagree, in Pickthall's translation: "and if ye have a dispute concerning any matter, refer it to Allah and the messenger". In practice, for Muslims, that means the Qur'an and the sunnah, the example of the Prophet, peace be upon him. The source. Second, the Prophet framed it the same way. In the Muwatta of Imam Malik, he is reported to have said he left two things, and as long as people hold to them they won't go astray: the Book of God and his sunnah. Third, the history. We've met a hadith promising a renewer for the community at the head of every hundred years, and we've met the people later generations called renewers. Al-Ghazali named a work the Revival of the Religious Sciences. Shah Wali Allah of Delhi put the Qur'an into Persian so ordinary readers could reach it themselves. The reformers of Cairo urged Muslims to read the text again with open minds. Different centuries, different lands, the same direction: upstream. Fourth, an honest note. Renewers didn't agree on what they found at the spring. Some stressed the law, some the inner life, some education, some politics, and they argued with each other, sometimes bitterly. Many scholars hold that the schools of law and the long chain of teachers are how a believer reaches the spring safely, not silt in the river; others called for reading the sources more directly. Returning to the source didn't end the disagreement. It gave everyone the same place to stand while they had it. And it leaves a habit for a single life: when things get muddy, go back to the text itself, not someone's summary of it.
screen: `REFER IT TO ALLAH AND THE MESSENGER.` · `THE BOOK AND THE SUNNAH: TWO THINGS LEFT.` · `RENEWERS WALK UPSTREAM.` · `THEY DISAGREED AT THE SPRING, TOO.`

segments.voice: The practice: read a page of Qur'an. If you have one nearby, in Arabic or in translation, open it anywhere, or at the beginning. Settle, and breathe. Read slowly, a line at a time, as if no one had ever explained it to you. Don't hunt for meaning yet. Just let the words themselves come first. If you don't have one with you, say the opening surah to yourself, or simply its first line, in the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful, and listen to it as if for the first time. The bell holds the time.
Returning to the source. Renewal in Islam keeps going back to the Qur'an and the sunnah, upstream to the spring. Today's word.
Your line: back to the source. Today, when you hear a claim about what Islam says, look up the verse or the hadith itself before you repeat it. Day one thousand fifty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims turn to the Qur'an and the sunnah as the final reference in matters of faith and practice, read through scholars and the schools of law that interpret them, and some read a portion of the Qur'an daily.

fork.reveal: the verse says to refer a dispute to Allah and the messenger, and that's where renewers kept returning.

trapdoor: what you thought: religious renewal means modernizing, changing the faith.
what it means: in Islam, renewal keeps meaning a return upstream to the Qur'an and the sunnah.
what a scholar hears: 4:59 and the Muwatta's two things left; al-Ghazali's Ihya, literally a revival; and renewers who disagreed about what they found.

Muwatta 'two things' hadith paraphrased; confirm reference (Book 46, Hadith 3) and that it is a mursal report (balaghan) in the Muwatta.
Abu Dawud 4291 (taught on day 1021) is referred back to; 'hundred years' is the hadith's own wording.
Shah Wali Allah's Persian translation of the Qur'an: well documented, but no date given; confirm.
Index hook says 'every renewal returned'; the script says 'they keep walking upstream' and adds that renewers disagreed, to avoid the sweeping claim.
Editor: cut the superlatives 'every court' (review) and 'his great work' (teach).

Audit: the muddy-river image ('silt, runoff, everything the town has thrown in'), 'not only what grandfather said', 'upstream past the silt' and the practice's 'not the commentary' together cast the inherited scholarship and the schools of law as pollution, which takes the reformist side in a live Sunni debate. Softened: the river now just 'picks up a lot along the way', the dismissive lines are cut, and the fourth turn says many scholars see the schools and chains of teachers as the way to the spring while others called for reading the sources more directly. Keeper (ideally one traditional, one reform-minded) should check balance.
